name: Priya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Priya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'm a bit nervous, to be honest, because I'm not the person at the office who has opinions about technology. I just do the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Hollins & Webb, a firm of about forty people near the station, and I do year-end accounts and personal tax returns for small businesses: cafés, hairdressers, a couple of builders. Most mornings I'm matching bank statements against what the client sent us, line by line, with a highlighter, which everyone teases me about. I like the moment a set of accounts finally balances, but the January tax rush wears me out, and I still need my senior, Ruth, to check most of what I do. I failed one of my professional exam papers last spring, so I'm resitting it in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like a relief. Everyone at work has been talking about the new bookkeeping software for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, quietly, at lunch. I'd say the hype was mostly people selling software to partners who wanted to cut costs. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be a bit uneasy, because the routine bits AI does take over are exactly my bits. Bank matching and coding receipts are most of my week. If the software does even half of that, Ruth will have more time and I'll have less to show for myself at review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and focus on passing my resit in March, because that's what really decides my pay. I'd keep putting about a fifth of my salary into savings like I do now. Maybe I'd let Ruth show me the matching tool, once, but I'd still check its work by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small knot in my stomach. The money side is fine, because Tomasz and I split the rent and I've got my gran's money put away. It's the being slow that bothers me, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still check the software by hand. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust what I can't see. Last year a client's card payments came through twice in a feed and nobody noticed until I did, with my highlighter. That's the one time anyone at work said I was good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your review at work actually look at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hours billed and how many returns I get out the door. If a tool does the matching, my hours look worse, even if my checking is better. That's the bit that's unfair and nobody talks about.

say: I'd say the AI **hype** was mostly software firms selling to partners who wanted **cheaper staff**.
I'd keep it to lunchtime chats and **not post** anything online.
think: The routine tasks AI takes are **my tasks**: bank matching and coding receipts.
My **review** counts hours billed, so a faster tool makes my **slow hands** look worse.
do: Keep doing accounts the **same way** and pass my **March resit**.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of my salary, as I already do.
Let my senior show me the **matching tool** once, then check it by hand.
feel: Mostly **calm** about money, with a small **knot** about being slow.
S0.quote: If a tool does the matching, my hours look worse, even if my checking is better.
fieldNote: Her **money** is secure, but her day is mostly the **routine** screen work even a plateau touches.
She takes pride in **catching errors** by hand and fears that skill stops being counted.
Resistance here is about **trust**, not laziness: she wants to see the working.

steps.text: Pass the resit of the failed professional exam paper in March
Keep putting a fifth of each pay packet into savings
Keep matching bank statements by hand and checking the new software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels close. Some of that is already starting at Hollins & Webb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk to the partners about what happens to juniors, and I'd say it in the staff meeting, not just at lunch. With friends I'd say this is what unions are for. My mum was a union rep at the council for twenty years and she'd be on the phone to me the same night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the people the firm wouldn't replace. Writing, checking and booking is basically my job description. They stopped hiring a junior last summer, and Ruth is already doing two people's reviews with the software helping her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the professional staff union this month, even though hardly anyone at a private firm does. I'd ask Ruth straight out where juniors fit in a year. And I'd start looking at the tax office, the government one, because public jobs move slower and they still train people properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit cornered. I hate that the answer everyone gives is learn the tools, because I'm bad at that and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, who started the same week as me. He's quicker than me but he's got a student loan and his mum relies on him. I've got a cushion, and if they cut one of us I honestly think he'd be in worse trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at the government tax office. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a few thousand a year in pay, because Hollins pays above the going rate. I could live with that. I'd rather earn a bit less somewhere that won't drop me the minute a cheaper tool appears.

say: I'd ask the partners in the **staff meeting** what happens to **juniors**.
I'd tell friends this is exactly what **unions** are for, like my mum always said.
think: Writing, checking and booking is my whole **job description**, so I'm exposed.
The firm already **stopped hiring** a junior, and my senior covers two reviews with software.
do: Join the **professional staff union** this month, even if few colleagues do.
Ask my senior directly where **juniors fit** in a year's time.
Apply to the **government tax office**, accepting a few thousand less in pay.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit **cornered** by being told to just learn the tools.
S1.quote: I'd rather earn a bit less somewhere that won't drop me the minute a cheaper tool appears.
fieldNote: Her progressive outlook shows in reaching for the **union** before anything else.
She worries more for a **colleague** with debts than for herself, knowing her cushion is strong.
She'd swap **pay** for **security**, choosing the slower public sector over learning AI.

steps.text: Join the professional staff union this month
Apply for a junior post at the government tax office
Keep the savings untouched in case the firm cuts juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh. That's before I'd even be fully qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in, properly, with some sort of income guarantee and limits on firms sacking everyone at once. I'd say it at work and I'd probably finally post something, which tells you how serious it would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it really means is my job goes, and probably by the end of 2028. Tax returns for a hairdresser are pure thinking work, no hands involved. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because there's nothing hands-on about what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop spending on anything big, and Tomasz and I would shelve the idea of buying a flat next year. I'd use my savings as runway and look at retraining into something hands-on, maybe nursing like Tomasz, because that buys me those three extra years and more. I'd go to every union and local meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you might be keeping us for a while, and I hate that. He'd say it's fine, he always says it's fine. But I grew up with my mum paying for everything and I promised myself I'd pull my weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nursing. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I faint at blood tests, which is a bit of a problem. But I'd rather do something with my hands and people than sit and watch a screen do the thing I spent four years learning.

say: I'd call for a **government income guarantee** and limits on mass sackings.
I'd finally **post online**, which shows how serious it feels.
think: My job likely **goes by 2028**, because tax returns are pure thinking work.
The **three-year robot gap** gives me nothing, since none of my work is hands-on.
do: Shelve the plan to **buy a flat** with my partner next year.
Use savings as **runway** while looking at **retraining** in hands-on care work like nursing.
Attend **union and local meetings** about income support.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing sums about the household.
S2.quote: I'd rather do something with my hands and people than sit and watch a screen do the thing I spent four years learning.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her work has **no hands-on part**, so the robot delay offers nothing.
Pride about **pulling her weight** at home matters as much as the money itself.
Her retraining idea, **nursing**, is half real and half hope; she faints at blood tests.

steps.text: Shelve buying a flat with her partner next year
Look into a nursing course to start before 2028
Go to union and local meetings pushing for an income guarantee
Stop all big purchases and live off one salary where possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least I'd be qualified by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, that we need rules and a safety net, but I'd say it louder because there'd be time to actually win something. I'd want the professional body to push for it too, not just the unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'd probably get qualified and then lose it a couple of years later. Spending the money and the exam stress on a job with a sell-by date is almost worse than losing it straight away. But it's better than two years because I could switch properly instead of panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the resit in March anyway, because a qualification still opens doors in the next few years. Then by 2028 I'd start a proper retraining course, something hands-on with people, while I'm still earning. I'd save hard so Tomasz isn't carrying me while I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but less trapped than with two years. There's time to make a plan, which is the thing I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said qualifying could be almost worse. Would you still sit the exam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because my mum would kill me if I didn't. And because for three or four years, a qualified accountant still earns more than an unqualified one. I'd just stop thinking of it as a career for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if you start saving hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holidays. Tomasz and I go somewhere warm every February after the tax rush, and that would be the first thing to go. I'd also stop the gym, which I never go to anyway.

say: I'd push for **a safety net**, louder, because five years leaves time to win.
I'd want the **professional body** to back it, not just the unions.
think: I'd likely get **qualified** and then lose the job a couple of years later.
Five years lets me **switch properly** instead of panicking like with two years.
do: Sit the **March resit** anyway, since qualified staff earn more for a few years.
Start a **hands-on retraining** course by **2028** while still earning.
Drop the **February holiday** and the gym to save harder.
feel: **Worried**, but less **trapped** than with two years.
S3.quote: Spending the money and the exam stress on a job with a sell-by date is almost worse than losing it straight away.
fieldNote: She still **expects to lose** the job; the extra years only change how she leaves.
She treats her **qualification** as a short-term pay bump, not a career.
Family pressure from her **mum** keeps her on the exam path even with doubts.

steps.text: Sit the resit of the professional exam in March
Start a hands-on retraining course in care work by 2028
Put the February holiday money into savings instead
Ask the professional body to back a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is enough time for governments to plan pensions, retraining money and a basic income, and if they don't, that's a choice. I'd keep saying that at work until people got bored of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have about seven good years as an accountant, maybe make it to senior, and then it ends anyway. That's not nothing. I'd just want to leave on my own timing and not be the last one switching off the lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, get some years of good pay in, and keep saving most of the difference. Around 2030 I'd start training for something in care or teaching, part-time, so I'm ready to move before the thinking work goes. And I'd stay in the union the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years with a deadline is like knowing your building will be knocked down, just not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd do with Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we'd probably still buy the flat, just a smaller one, and keep a big buffer. And we'd talk about kids differently. I'd want a job that still exists before we start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd have to, a bit, just to keep my job for those seven years. I'd learn the minimum. I'm not going to become one of those people who's excited about it.

say: I'd say ten years leaves governments **no excuse** not to plan retraining and income.
I'd keep raising it at work until colleagues got bored.
think: I'd get about **seven good years**, maybe reach senior, then the job ends anyway.
I want to leave on **my own timing**, not be the last one out.
do: Qualify and **bank the higher pay**, saving most of the difference.
Start **part-time training** in care or teaching around **2030**.
Learn the **minimum** of the AI tools to keep the job meanwhile.
feel: **Calmer** but not calm, like a building scheduled for **demolition**.
S4.quote: Ten years with a deadline is like knowing your building will be knocked down, just not yet.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts her from fear to **planning**, but she still expects the job to **end**.
Family plans like **children** now hinge on having a job that will last.
She'd grudgingly **learn AI** tools, only to buy time.

steps.text: Save most of the pay rise after qualifying
Start part-time training in care or teaching around 2030
Learn the bookkeeping software just enough to stay useful
Buy a smaller flat and hold off on children until work is settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't long enough to retrain for anything, and my job is all screen. What would help is a government that pays for retraining while you do it, so people like Kwame aren't stuck, and firms having to give juniors a proper notice period.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the slow one. Everyone asks about the clever people losing out. The ones who learn a bit slower will get left first, and nobody designs these changes with us in mind.

headlineQuote: The ones who learn a bit slower will get left first, and nobody designs these changes with us in mind.
portrait: Priya is a **junior accountant** at a forty-person firm doing small-business accounts and tax returns.
She checks bank statements by hand, distrusts **software she can't see**, and never uses AI tools.
Her **savings** and her partner's nursing pay mean money isn't the fear; being the slow one is.
She reaches first for **unions** and government help, and moves from uneasy to **alarmed** as AGI arrives sooner.
Her escape plan is **hands-on care work**, though she admits she faints at blood tests.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to **retrain** and her job is all screen.
whatWouldHelp: Government-paid **retraining** while studying, and a proper **notice period** for juniors.
